## Answer (researched 2026-10-15 from the primary docs)

**Short version: nothing to build.** The only real overlap is a proprietary Moderne feature (Prethink) that computes the same package-level metrics archy does, as agent context and dashboards rather than as a gate. For a Python codebase, open-source OpenRewrite is not available in any form that substitutes for a subscription, and archy already covers the read-only analysis part.

### What OpenRewrite gives you for free, and from Python

- **Apache 2.0:** the core framework, the Java/Groovy/Kotlin/XML/YAML/Properties/HCL modules, building-block recipes (`ChangeType` and similar), and the Maven/Gradle plugins. ([licensing](https://docs.openrewrite.org/licensing/openrewrite-licensing))
- **Moderne Source Available License (MSAL):** every newer language module, Python included (`rewrite-python`, also JS/TS, C#, Go, Ruby, Scala), plus the big recipe modules (`rewrite-spring`, `rewrite-static-analysis`, `rewrite-migrate-java`, ...). You may run them on your own code; you may not put them in a commercial product. ([module table](https://docs.openrewrite.org/reference/latest-versions-of-every-openrewrite-module))
- **Proprietary, customers only:** extra languages, the newest framework upgrades, Prethink, impact analysis.
- **Python specifically:** `rewrite-python` describes itself as "work-in-progress" and "only supported via the Moderne CLI or the Moderne Platform", not the Maven/Gradle plugins. The CLI "is free to use for open-source repositories"; closed-source repos need a license. ([rewrite-python README](https://github.com/openrewrite/rewrite-python)) Python recipes exist but are migration-shaped (for example `UpgradeToPython38`).
- Recipe distribution is moving to Moderne's own repository, where MSAL and proprietary recipes are "available to customers only". ([Code Genome Project](https://docs.moderne.io/user-documentation/recipes/accessing-the-code-genome-project/)) That sits awkwardly with the OpenRewrite FAQ's statement that OSS projects may run MSAL recipes; I did not resolve it.

### Moderne capabilities absent from archy

| Capability | Tag |
|---|---|
| Lossless, type-attributed semantic tree (LST) plus format-preserving rewrite | out of scope (archy does not edit code) |
| Recipe catalogue and recipe execution | out of scope |
| Fleet-wide LST pre-build, multi-repo recipe runs, mass commits/PRs | out of scope (archy is single-repo, by design) |
| Cross-repo search and impact analysis ("what does this touch across 100k repos") | plausible in principle; no signal |
| Symbol-level lookup tools in MCP (`find_types`, `find_methods`, `find_implementations`, trigram search) | out of scope (module granularity was settled in #316; these are navigation tools) |
| MCP edit tools (`change_type`, `pattern_replace`, `edit_code`) | out of scope |
| Prethink: generated `.moderne/context/` files with architecture, dependency usage, test gaps, package coupling/instability/abstractness, cycle detection, CBO/LCOM4 | **already have it** in substance: `archy brief`, `conventions --emit-headers`, `score`, `cycles`, `dsm`. archy's version is open source and works on Python; Prethink is proprietary and Java-first |
| Single-repo impact before a change | already have it (`impact`, `simulate`, `affected`, `diff`) |
| Deterministic output | already have it |

One more thing archy has and Moderne does not, as far as either doc set shows: **enforcement**. Moderne computes cycles and coupling but has no layer-rule DSL and no CI gate on the dependency graph. archy's `check` / `cycles --strict` / `diff` gating is the differentiator, not determinism.

### Usage signal for the one plausible item

None. Every issue in this repo that mentions multi-repo, fleet, cross-repo, codemods, OpenRewrite or Moderne was filed by the maintainer (#316, #361, this ticket). The usage baseline stands at fewer than 20 real users. **Recommendation: don't build cross-repo impact.**

### Point 4: say "deterministic" in the README?

No. Moderne's determinism pitch contrasts its *edits* with LLM edits; archy makes no edits, so the contrast does not transfer. archy's honest differentiator, for anyone comparing the two, is that it gates structure in CI, which Moderne does not do. That is already what the README leads with.

### The user's framing: which parts of a Moderne subscription could archy plus open-source OpenRewrite replace?

- **Python codebase:** OpenRewrite does not apply in open-source form (Python support is MSAL and CLI-only, free only for OSS repos), and Moderne's published prices ([pricing](https://www.moderne.ai/pricing): typical Commercial $250K, Enterprise $2M, Fully Managed $5M) are for code transformation at fleet scale. archy replaces the architecture-metrics slice (Prethink's package metrics, cycle detection) and adds gating. It replaces none of the transformation, which is what the bill is mostly for.
- **Java codebase:** open-source OpenRewrite plus the Maven/Gradle plugins covers single-repo transformation with Apache-licensed recipes. archy is not involved (Python-only).

### Claims from the original ticket that did not survive checking

- **The Log4Shell figure (400 repos, 38,000 call sites, zero regressions)** traces only to a third-party roundup ([pixelmatters](https://www.pixelmatters.com/insights/application-modernization-software)), whose link to moderne.ai/openrewrite does not contain it. Do not cite it.
- **"Pricing page 404s":** it exists now and publishes typical prices.
- **"Moderne doesn't do architecture analysis":** Prethink does compute package coupling and cycles, but descriptively.

Moderne's own MCP docs say of their tools that "agents don't call them consistently" ([mcp overview](https://docs.moderne.io/user-documentation/agent-tools/mcp/overview/)). That matches archy's six-null delivery line from the other side, and it is not a reason to try a seventh.

The ticket's Notes say the repo is in maintenance; that is out of date (archy is active again). It does not change the answer: nothing here clears the usage-signal gate.

Closing as answered. No follow-up tickets filed.

input.description: Read issue #386

content.content:
**Source:** [The Economic Benefit of Refactoring](https://martinfowler.com/articles/exploring-gen-ai/refactoring-economic-benefit.html), Giles Edwards-Alexander (Thoughtworks), 30 July 2026, in Fowler's *Exploring Gen AI* series.

Research-only. **No feature work is proposed here**, and per the 2026-07-27 wind-down (`docs/WHAT_DIDNT_WORK.md`) none should be until this question is answered.

## Setting

A ~150 kLoC app (~120 kLoC Rust, rest TypeScript and Terraform) written **entirely by agents** (mostly Claude Code, some Cursor), whose author states he did not read or review the code except occasionally. Its data access layer grew unchecked to a single **17,155-line Rust file**: no de-duplication, no internal language, limited function extraction, very little class extraction, but a clear boundary and an interface to preserve.

## Method

Refactor in steps; after *every* step, run the *same* representative feature-change prompt in a **fresh sub-agent**, record cost, then throw the change away. Fresh agents never learn, so each step is an independent, uncontaminated measurement of "what does this change cost now?" That property is the reason the design works at all, and it is the part most worth stealing.

## Results

| Step | DAL LoC | Largest file LoC | Input tokens | Output tokens | Time (s) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Baseline | 17,155 | 17,155 | 159,564 | 1,705 | **342** |
| Step 1 (FirestoreClient) | 16,706 | 16,706 | 155,205 | 1,723 | 530 |
| Step 5 (value ctors) | 16,469 | 16,469 | **171,251** | 2,036 | **1,353** |
| Step 6 (FieldsBuilder) | 16,469 | 16,469 | 171,251 | 2,036 | 1,353 |
| Step 7 (queries.rs) | 16,474 | 15,670 | 151,850 | 1,800 | 587 |
| Step 12 (store/ split) | 16,550 | 9,269 | 104,080 | 2,050 | 490 |
| Step 15 (store/ split) | 16,608 | **3,695** | **27,360** | 2,113 | **454** |

**Input tokens: 159,564 -> 27,360, a saving of 132,204 or -83%.** At Sonnet 5 $3/MTok that is **39.7 cents per change**, and the author is careful to call that "not a lot" and to ask openly whether it multiplies.

Four things in that table matter more than the headline:

1. **Total LoC is flat** (50,359 -> 49,812 Rust total; the DAL itself rises 17,155 -> 16,608 across 19 files). Nothing was deleted. The saving is that the agent **reads** less, not that there **is** less.
2. **The effect tracks largest-file LoC only.** Input tokens are flat while the largest file is flat, and fall as it falls, "off a cliff" at the end.
3. **Output tokens went up**, 1,705 -> 2,113, and wander non-monotonically throughout. The saving is entirely on the input side.
4. **Time per change went UP, not down: 342s baseline -> 454s final**, peaking at 1,353s mid-run. The article's closing claim is that the effort "shows the value, in time and money of refactoring", but **its own table shows the time column moving the wrong way**, and this is never addressed. Any replication must decide in advance whether wall-clock is an outcome; if it is, this result is currently a *mixed* one, not a win. (The author notes the run was on slow hotel WiFi, which is an uncontrolled confound on exactly this column.)

## The author's causal claim, which is not "split big files"

This is the part most easily misread, including by me on a first pass. The early steps (1-6, extract function / extract class) **did not move input tokens** and step 5 moved them backwards. But the author does not conclude they were wasted:

> "...the earlier refactorings were necessary to set up this saving. This was not planned. It was simply a result of how refactoring typically proceeds: local file changes to extract duplication, before breaking down into smaller files once a repeating core emerges."

And on why size alone is not the lever:

> "randomly cutting the file into smaller files is unlikely to help as much: even if each file were smaller, the agent would be forced to read through many files looking for the relevant code."

So the claimed mechanism is **locatability**, not size: the agent can bank the saving only if it can identify the smallest sufficient subset of files to read. Evidence offered is the metric curve plus reading Claude Code's thinking output and file-read summaries, which showed progressively smaller reads. That is observational, not instrumented.

**This kills the naive feature idea before it is written down.** "Rank files by LoC and tell the agent to split them" is precisely the random-cutting the author predicts will not work, and it skips the de-duplication phase he says was the precondition.

## The other finding, which is arguably the more relevant one to archy

From "Notes on the process", entirely separate from the token result:

- **"Claude was not good at refactoring."** It cannot look at code, consider refactorings in general, and work out which apply. A human had to actively guide it; the refactorings produced were direct responses to the prompt.
- **The app's development harness already includes an explicit refactoring step, and that step never prompted Claude to improve this file.** A 17k-line god file grew under a harness that was supposed to catch exactly this.
- Claude.ai beat Claude Code at *planning* the refactor: Claude Code proposed extract-function first, Claude.ai saw the whole client class to extract.
- Applying the refactorings was also bad: done via Python grep/sed scripts that "frequently got confused by indentation", and **the single most valuable refactoring was missed in the first pass** and had to be re-applied later.

An agent that cannot *notice* a 17,155-line file is a target, under a harness explicitly told to look, is a target-identification failure. That is closer to what archy's `what_to_refactor_next` claims to do than anything about tokens, and it is a claim archy has never tested.

## Why this is worth a ticket rather than dismissing

archy already NO-GO'd the token-reduction category (#314/#315, `docs/research/TOKEN_REDUCTION_CLAIMS.md`), and archy's own Experiment 1 (#282/#289) is a direct near-contradiction:

> Apply archy's #1 `what-to-refactor-next` target to Flask, run the same task against both variants, N=10 interleaved pairs. `file_revisitations` -1.0 at a 5/5 split, sign p=1.000. `footprint_tokens` **+4,213**, leaning the wrong way.

Same question, opposite answer. Candidate reconciliations, which is what this ticket exists to test:

1. **Headroom.** Flask's #1 target is a normal-sized module in a mature, already-decomposed library; the article's baseline was a 17k-line god file in agent-written greenfield code. archy's null may be a measurement taken at zero headroom, the same binding constraint that capped #282, #289, #356 and #369.
2. **Wrong lens.** `what_to_refactor_next` fuses CC x churn and structural `edit_risk`. **Neither lens sees file size or duplication**, which are the two variables the article implicates. archy pointed Flask at the class of refactor (steps 1-6) that the article measured as moving nothing on its own.
3. **Task class.** #315 established that a graph is an *answer* for architecture questions and only a *hint* for edits. This is an edit task, archy's weak class, and it still found a large effect. That is the part that does not fit the existing story.

## The question to answer

**Does the token-per-change curve depend on largest-file LoC, and does it have a knee?** Is there a size threshold above which decomposition reliably pays back and below which it does nothing, which would explain the Flask null exactly?

Secondary, and possibly the better question: **is the mechanism size or locatability?** These are separable by design. Split a god file two ways, once along cohesive seams and once arbitrarily at line boundaries, holding largest-file LoC equal. If size is the lever, both arms drop equally. If locatability is the lever, only the cohesive arm drops. **The article asserts this distinction but did not test it**, and it is cheap to test.

If either comes back positive, archy has one defensible thing it does not do: rank candidates by agent read cost rather than by CC x churn. If not, this closes as a seventh null and the wind-down stands unamended.

## Before designing anything, read

- `docs/WHAT_DIDNT_WORK.md`, all six studies, especially Experiment 1.
- `docs/research/TOKEN_REDUCTION_CLAIMS.md` and its §10 correction log (16 items).
- CLAUDE.md, "Measurement and benches". This is *precisely* the paper-motivated shape the anti-theater rule warns about, and it must clear that gate before it clears anything else.

## Design constraints this study inherits, non-negotiable

- **Pilot the control arm before fixing a threshold.** #369's win condition was arithmetically unreachable before the run started because the control rate was assumed rather than measured. Here: measure baseline token cost on the candidate repo at N>=5 first, *then* fix the threshold.
- **Pre-register the thresholds, including the ones that kill the idea.** Obvious null-killer: if input tokens do not move by >= X% between largest-file-LoC extremes, it is a null and gets written up as one.
- **N > 1 per step.** The source has a single sub-agent run per step and therefore no variance estimate at all; the non-monotonic wobble in both the token and time columns is unquantified noise. Repeat runs per step are mandatory.
- **Checkpoint per unit and resume.** Copy `bench/_supervise.py` / `bench/q1b_run.py`; `tests/test_q1b_run.py` pins the rules.
- **Audit for artifact-shaped numbers.** The decay study carried six, and every one biased toward the wanted answer.

## Known weaknesses of the source, inherited by any replication

- **n=1 everywhere.** One file, one repo, one representative change, one developer, one run per step, greenfield.
- **The refactoring cost was never measured.** The author says so plainly: he did not think to count until it was over, the upper bound is **five million tokens**, and that bound also covers building the refactoring plan twice plus designing the experiment. So the "economic benefit" headline reports a return with no investment figure. At 39.7 cents saved per change, payback against a 5M-token upper bound needs on the order of 10^4 changes to the DAL. **A replication that does not measure refactoring cost answers the read-cost question but not the economic one**, and should not use the word "economic".
- **Token counts are a proxy.** The author reports Claude gives no reliable live token counting, so the sub-agent reported **characters received**, converted. Any effect smaller than the char-to-token ratio error is not resolvable.
- **Three pairs of identical rows** (5/6, 8/9, 12/13) are byte-identical across input tokens, output tokens *and* time. That is artifact-shaped by the `WHAT_DIDNT_WORK` standard. The author's note that "the number of steps in the figure don't match the refactoring steps in the appendix" (because the most valuable refactoring was missed and re-applied) is a candidate explanation, i.e. carried-forward rows for steps that changed no file boundary, but it is not stated and should not be assumed.
- **The final largest file is a test library, not production code.** By the end the DAL is 19 files and the biggest remaining one is tests. How much of the final cliff is "production code got locatable" versus "the remaining bulk is test code the agent can skip" is not separated.
- **Wall-clock is confounded** by admitted slow hotel WiFi over an ~8-hour mostly-unattended run, with one manual intervention at 6h40m when a step had been skipped.
- **Best case for the mechanism throughout:** Rust, a single self-contained module, a clean preserved interface, and a codebase with no human review history to constrain the refactor.

## Out of scope for this ticket

Filing feature tickets. Nothing gets built off an n=1 external result; #315 is the precedent for closing a research ticket NO-GO with no tickets filed, and that remains the most likely outcome here.

The agent-footprint minimal-pair research line is **closed** (epic #259 closed
2026-07-24), with two nulls (#289 arm C N=22, #282 flask N=10) and one cell
(#300 rich) cancelled by pre-run adversarial review before any agent time.

**Why it will not be reopened as-is:** the design is structurally unable to
produce an interpretable *positive* result at that scale. A treatment strong
enough to move the metric relocates the task's answer into a smaller file, so a
positive reads as relocation; a treatment conservative enough to avoid that is
attackable as too weak a dose. One repo, one task, N=10, one model cannot escape
that squeeze.

**Do not propose another hand-built pair.** A future attempt needs many repos and
tasks, or a naturally-occurring before/after corpus.

**What survives:** `what_to_refactor_next` stands on human maintainability and
edit risk, which this bench never measured. What is ruled out is the *claim* that
archy cuts an agent's token bill. The harness itself is sound and reusable
(39 tests, counterbalanced pairing, per-run reset, measured baselines, provenance
checks, canonical variant-neutral metrics, harness-owned publication pinned by a
golden test).

Writeup: `bench/agent_footprint_results.md`. Protocol:
`docs/SPEC_AGENT_FOOTPRINT_BENCH.md`. Related: [[feedback-use-deepwork-review]],
[[project-archy-next-up]].

## Desk answer (2026-10-15), before any agent time

**The "same question, opposite answer" contradiction with Experiment 1 dissolves on the numbers alone.** Experiment 1 never left the region where the article itself measured no effect.

| | Largest-file LoC, before -> after | Input-token effect |
|---|---|---|
| Article, steps 1-6 | 17,155 -> 16,469 | flat; step 5 went backwards (+7%) |
| Article, step 7 | 16,469 -> 15,670 | -5% (151,850 vs 159,564) |
| Article, step 15 (end) | -> 3,695 | -83% |
| archy Experiment 1 (#282, Flask) | `sansio/app.py` 1,013 -> 611 | null (`footprint_tokens` +4,213, wrong way) |

Experiment 1's *starting* file is 3.6x smaller than the article's *finishing* file. If the curve has a knee, it lies somewhere above ~3.7k lines, because the article's last measured point (3,695) is where its effect had already been banked. Flask sat an order of magnitude below that before the refactor began. Reconciliation 1 (headroom) is therefore not just plausible, it is the only reading the two datasets jointly allow. No contradiction remains to be resolved by a run.

A mechanical reason the knee could sit in that range, offered as a hypothesis and not tested here: Claude Code's `Read` returns at most 2,000 lines per call, so a file above that size forces paged reads or grep-then-read, while a file below it costs one read. Flask's 1,013-line file was a single read before and after.

## Should the knee or the locatability question be measured?

**Recommendation: no.** Three reasons, each sufficient alone:

1. **It is the closed footprint design.** The cohesive-vs-arbitrary split is a hand-built minimal pair on one repo, one task and one model: exactly the shape the #259 epic closed on 2026-07-24. A positive in the cohesive arm reads as relocation of the answer into a smaller file, which is what "locatability" *is*. The squeeze that killed #300 applies unchanged.
2. **A positive would not implicate archy.** The question is about the codebase, not about archy. The only feature a positive could motivate is "rank by largest-file LoC" (or "by read cost"). `wc -l | sort -n` already does that, so the feature would fail the anti-theater test whatever the bench says.
3. **No usage signal.** No user has asked for read-cost ranking, and the usage baseline is under 20 real users. A multi-hour paid bench needs a reason beyond an n=1 external post.

## What this changes

- **Experiment 1 stands, with a sharper caveat.** Its null holds for modules of ~1k lines. It says nothing about god files in the 10k+ range, and `docs/WHAT_DIDNT_WORK.md` should not be read as saying it does.
- **`what_to_refactor_next` is still blind to file size and duplication** (reconciliation 2). That observation is true, but it is the same feature idea with the same gate, so nothing is filed.
- **The "Claude did not notice the target" finding** (the article's harness had a refactoring step that never flagged a 17k-line file) is the closest thing here to an archy claim. Testing whether archy would have flagged it needs the article's code, which is not public. Not actionable.

Unless someone wants to fund the bench, this closes NO-GO on desk analysis, in the same way as #315, with no follow-up tickets.

content.content:
## What

Investigate emitting [archify](https://github.com/tt-a1i/archify) architecture IR from archy, so a repository's structure and its drift between two snapshots can be published as an interactive, explorable artifact.

Split out of #399, which chose `diagram-design` for static editorial docs art and explicitly scopes generated diagrams out. This is the other half of that seam:

- **diagram-design** (#399): hand-authored, high-altitude, static, embedded in README and `docs/*.md`.
- **archify** (this ticket): generated from archy's own output, interactive, on a linked standalone page.

Keeping them apart is deliberate. Mixing both inside the docs would give archy two visual languages.

## Why it is interesting

`archify compare architecture <base>.json <head>.json` emits a structured delta, not just a picture. Run against its own example pair it returns:

```
components:  added 1, removed 1, changed 1, moved 1
connections: added 1, removed 1, changed 2, rerouted 1
plus: receipt, proofLevel, completeness
```

That is conceptually the job `archy snapshot` + `archy diff` already do. archy produces the two snapshots; archify renders the delta as something a human governor can explore. The fit is real, which is why this is worth recording rather than dropping.

archify is MIT, actively maintained, and its renderer is zero-dependency Node with a CLI (`archify render|validate|compare`).

## The blocker, measured first

**archify will not solve layout for you, and that is its design stance.** It validates that geometry is truthful and rejects anything that is not. Any generator has to produce placement and routing that survives those checks.

Tested against a real 9-node, 17-edge archy subgraph (`cli`, `mcp`, `contracts`, `conventions`, `score`, `cycles`, `layers`, `graph`, `parser`), using archify's `layout.mode: "grid"` with `row`/`col` auto-placement:

| Attempt | Errors |
|---|---|
| Naive rank assignment | 4 |
| Crossing-minimized column order | 2 |

Both survivors are the same class:

```
[clean-flow/edge-through-node] "cli" -> "layers" crosses component "contracts"
  (unrelated to this relationship) on segment 0 (2px clearance)
```

These are rank-skipping edges passing through an intervening node: the standard problem that layered graph drawing solves with dummy nodes and lane assignment (Sugiyama). Getting to zero means implementing that in the generator.

Scale makes it harder, not easier. That test used 9 nodes. archy parses 201 nodes and 864 edges in its own repository, and even at package altitude the fan-out is heavy (`archy.cli` has 7 outgoing edges in the subgraph above, `archy.mcp` has 6).

## The question to answer before any code

**Is a Sugiyama-style router worth building to feed a third-party renderer?**

Arguments that it is not:
- archy is in active development, but not in this direction. What it does today is one thing: turn a Python import and call graph into answers an agent can act on between edits (blast radius, affected tests, cycles, layer rules that fail CI, a five-axis score, and a snapshot/diff loop that catches structure regressing silently), as a CLI and an MCP server off one graph. Where it is going is *deeper into that loop rather than wider*: the measured failure mode is delivery and retrieval, not capability, so the standing design rule is to put answers in the DEFAULT OUTPUT of commands already being run instead of adding surfaces to discover. The live threads are the vacuity family (a check that could not have failed must not report like one that held) and the two structural refactors, #389 and #395. A separate interactive artifact on a linked page is a new surface with its own discovery problem, which is the argument this ticket has to beat.
- `archy render` already exists for visualization, and #399 found no usage signal driving this.
- The routing work is real, and it is work archify intentionally does not do.

Arguments that it might be:
- The snapshot/diff mapping is unusually clean, and drift-over-time is archy's actual thesis.
- It is additive: a new output format, no change to existing surfaces.

Per this repository's conventions this should go through the anti-theater test and be weighed against the usage-signal priority **before** anyone writes code. Filed to record the finding and the measurement, not as an endorsement.

## Not in scope

- Changing `archy render`'s existing output format.
- Replacing the #399 docs diagrams.
- Vendoring archify into this repository.

## Evidence

All numbers above were produced by running archify v2.17.0-dev.0 locally against archy's real dependency graph, not read from documentation.


---

## Addendum (2026-09-10): the system-graph half of the same idea

Added after reading Stéphane Derosiaux, ["Frontier AI: Claude Code and Codex Still Use grep. Why?"](https://levelup.gitconnected.com/claude-code-and-codex-still-search-code-like-its-1975-that-s-not-an-accident-8f70cb9897ea) (Sep 2026). Two of its points land on this ticket rather than on the docs tickets it also produced (#474, #475), because they are about what an artifact would *contain*, not about how a tool describes itself.

## What

Investigate emitting [archify](https://github.com/tt-a1i/archify) architecture IR from archy, so a repository's structure and its drift between two snapshots can be published as an interactive, explorable artifact.

Split out of #399, which chose `diagram-design` for static editorial docs art and explicitly scopes generated diagrams out. This is the other half of that seam:

- **diagram-design** (#399): hand-authored, high-altitude, static, embedded in README and `docs/*.md`.
- **archify** (this ticket): generated from archy's own output, interactive, on a linked standalone page.

Keeping them apart is deliberate. Mixing both inside the docs would give archy two visual languages.

## Why it is interesting

`archify compare architecture <base>.json <head>.json` emits a structured delta, not just a picture. Run against its own example pair it returns:

```
components:  added 1, removed 1, changed 1, moved 1
connections: added 1, removed 1, changed 2, rerouted 1
plus: receipt, proofLevel, completeness
```

That is conceptually the job `archy snapshot` + `archy diff` already do. archy produces the two snapshots; archify renders the delta as something a human governor can explore. The fit is real, which is why this is worth recording rather than dropping.

archify is MIT, actively maintained, and its renderer is zero-dependency Node with a CLI (`archify render|validate|compare`).

## The blocker, measured first

**archify will not solve layout for you, and that is its design stance.** It validates that geometry is truthful and rejects anything that is not. Any generator has to produce placement and routing that survives those checks.

Tested against a real 9-node, 17-edge archy subgraph (`cli`, `mcp`, `contracts`, `conventions`, `score`, `cycles`, `layers`, `graph`, `parser`), using archify's `layout.mode: "grid"` with `row`/`col` auto-placement:

| Attempt | Errors |
|---|---|
| Naive rank assignment | 4 |
| Crossing-minimized column order | 2 |

Both survivors are the same class:

```
[clean-flow/edge-through-node] "cli" -> "layers" crosses component "contracts"
  (unrelated to this relationship) on segment 0 (2px clearance)
```

These are rank-skipping edges passing through an intervening node: the standard problem that layered graph drawing solves with dummy nodes and lane assignment (Sugiyama). Getting to zero means implementing that in the generator.

- The snapshot/diff mapping is unusually clean, and drift-over-time is archy's actual thesis.

input.description: Read coupling module doc and hidden-coupling filter

content.content:
"""Change coupling (temporal coupling): module pairs that change together in
git history but share no import/call edge (advisory, not a score axis).

The import + call graph captures *structural* coupling. This captures
*behavioral* coupling (Gall et al.; Tornhill / CodeScene's logical-coupling
lineage, the same git history `archy hotspots` mines): two modules that change
together commit after commit yet have no edge between them signal a hidden
dependency or a missing abstraction the structural analysis cannot see. The
output is deliberately filtered to pairs the graph *misses* (no import/call edge
either direction), so it complements the graph rather than restating it, and the
framing is agent-actionable ("you're editing X; Y historically co-changes, check
Y").

Co-change is noisy: a single sweeping commit (a reformat, a mass rename, a
license-header pass) touches hundreds of files and would couple all of them.
Two defenses, both required before the signal is trustworthy:

* **Commit-size normalization** - a commit touching more than `max_commit_files`
  `.py` files is dropped entirely (from both the pair counts and the per-file
  denominators), so only focused commits vote. This is why `git_cochange`'s
    *,
    exclude: frozenset[str] = frozenset(),
    min_support: int = DEFAULT_MIN_SUPPORT,
    min_confidence: float = DEFAULT_MIN_CONFIDENCE,
) -> list[CoChangeHint]:
    """Modules that co-change with a `targets` set but have no structural edge to it.

    Reuses `compute_coupling`'s pair logic, then keeps each no-edge pair with
    exactly one endpoint in `targets` (a pair fully inside `targets` is two
    modules already being edited together, not a hint). The other endpoint is
    the hint; a partner in `exclude` (e.g. modules already in the blast radius)
    or itself a target is dropped, so hints surface only the *hidden* couplings.
    Ranked by `(-confidence, -support, module)`.
    """
    hints: list[CoChangeHint] = []
    for pair in compute_coupling(
        graph, cochange, min_support=min_support, min_confidence=min_confidence
    ):
        a_in, b_in = pair.module_a in targets, pair.module_b in targets
        if a_in == b_in:  # both edited, or neither a target: not a hint
            continue

  Render a view as a self-contained HTML file (offline, no JS, no CDN).

  `--view=dsm` draws the Design Structure Matrix, back-edges in red;
  `--view=trend` plots the five axes over .archy/history.jsonl. Output is

                                  than this.  [default: 300]

## Desk answer (2026-10-15): no-go, and the addendum's premise is already shipped

The ticket asks for the anti-theater test and the usage-signal weighing **before** any code. Both are answered below, and neither needs a hand-built artifact.

### The addendum's test case is not invisible

The addendum's concrete case is "a co-change edge with no import edge ... the one edge type that is invisible in every current surface". That has been false since #250 (2026-07-04, `src/archy/coupling.py`):

- `archy coupling` outputs **exactly** that edge type and nothing else. Its module docstring: "deliberately filtered to pairs the graph *misses* (no import/call edge either direction), so it complements the graph rather than restating it".
- `archy_impact(co_change=true)` hands the same hidden couplings to an agent inside a blast radius, with partners already in the radius dropped (`co_changed_with`, "so hints surface only the *hidden* couplings").

So the information exists on two surfaces, one of them the agent's default loop. The only thing missing is **drawing** it next to the import graph. That makes the scoped question "is a picture of three existing outputs worth a Sugiyama router and a new surface?", not "can a governor see something new?".

### The gates

- **Anti-theater:** fails. A node-link overlay of `check`, `coupling` and `diff` output restates three answers archy already gives as text and JSON. `archy render --help` records the earlier decision on the base case: "There is no `graph` view: a node-link diagram needs a vendored layout engine and carries the least signal of the three, so it stays deferred (docs/SPEC_VISUALIZATION.md)". archify does not remove that cost, because, as the measurement above shows, it refuses to lay out for you.
- **The repo's own design rule:** fails. The body already makes the case against it: answers go in the default output of commands already being run, not on a new surface with its own discovery problem. A linked standalone page is the clearest possible instance of that.
- **Usage signal:** none. No user has asked for an interactive architecture page or for drift visualisation beyond `render --view=trend`, and the baseline is under 20 real users.

### What would reopen it

A user asking to *see* structural drift between two snapshots, where `archy diff` text and `render --view=trend` demonstrably do not serve them. At that point, start from `snapshot` + `diff` -> `archify compare` (the clean mapping the body found), not from the system-graph overlay.

Recommend closing NO-GO, with no follow-up tickets.

=== #418
`bench/conventions_bench_results.md` predicted this feature and set a condition on it:

> **So the next change to this command is not a fifth census.** It is queryability: a `--module` filter, an exhaustive mode, or a lookup that answers "what consumes X" and "does X reach Y" on demand. 🔴 **And that should not be added to this PR**: the held-out set scores detection, so a retrieval feature would ship unmeasured, which is the failure this file exists to prevent. It needs its own held-out measurement, against derivations rather than repositories.

`--module` / `archy_module_view` shipped in #414. The first instruction held: it was kept out of #412 and landed in its own PR. The second did not. There is no held-out score for retrievability, so nothing in the repository currently says the lookup answers the derivations it was built for.

## Why the existing numbers do not cover it

The 15/15 development and 12/13 held-out figures score DETECTION: does the census find the conventions a repository actually has. Retrieval is a different question (given a derivation an agent needs, does the lookup return it), and the import-resolution helpers `--module` added are not on the path the census scores at all. Reading those numbers as evidence for `--module` would be exactly the artifact-shaped inference `docs/WHAT_DIDNT_WORK.md` warns about.

## What the measurement needs

Per the paragraph above, the unit is a DERIVATION, not a repository. The motivating evidence for the feature was 24 pieces of real agent reasoning scored against the ranked report, which scored 0 of 24; that set is the obvious starting point but is development data now, so a held-out set has to be drawn separately.

Pre-register the threshold before running, per AGENTS.md, including the value that kills the feature. Note the arithmetic trap from #369: fix the control rate by pilot, not by inference, or the win condition can be unreachable before the run starts.

## Scope

Measurement only. `--module` itself is shipped and its correctness is covered by unit tests; this is about whether it answers real derivations, which no test can tell us.
=== #480
## Summary

Research https://www.scbench.ai/ and assess how it could be used to build or improve archy.

## Questions to answer

- What does SCBench measure? (benchmark type, tasks, metrics)
- What is the target use case -- agent scaffolding, code quality, software engineering tasks, or something else?
- Does it measure anything archy already surfaces (layer violations, cycles, coupling, reachability)?
- Could archy's output be used as context/input to improve agent performance on SCBench tasks?
- Could SCBench be used to validate archy's own effectiveness (similar to the bench/ harness)?
- Are there specific SCBench tasks or metrics where archy's structural analysis would give a measurable lift?
- Does this pass the anti-theater test? (see `feedback_vet_proposals_anti_theater.md`)

## Constraints

- Check against the six-intervention null history before proposing any new bench cell (see `bench/` and `docs/WHAT_DIDNT_WORK.md`)
- If a new measurement is proposed, pre-register thresholds and pilot the control arm first
- Only file follow-up tickets if findings clear the OECD axis gate

## Out of scope for this ticket

Implementation -- this is research only.

Web research only, no code changes. Run `date` first and report it. Research https://www.scbench.ai/ (and any paper, GitHub repo, leaderboard or docs it links). content.content:
## 🔴 What this bench does NOT measure, and the measurement that says it matters

Everything above is **detection**: does the census derive the fact? The answer is yes,
12/13 held-out. That is not the same as **retrievability**: can a reader get the fact
out of the default output?

They came apart, and the gap was measured rather than guessed. 24 pieces of real agent
reasoning were selected *because* an inventory could in principle have stated the fact
they were working out (a deliberately favourable sample) and scored blind against this
build and against the previous release. Two independent readers, neither told which
version was which:

**0 of 24, both versions, perfect agreement on every row.**

Both readers gave the same reason without being prompted for one:

> every near-miss failed on **truncation**, not on the wrong kind of fact; the report
> says `150; showing 12`, so **absence from the list proves nothing**

Four blockers, none of which is "the census derives the wrong things":

1. **Truncation.** The section computes 150 families and prints 12. The fix above moves
   one co-update set from rank 38 to rank 4, which is why the `archy-at-eval-pin` row
   asserts `max_rank: 12`, but that guards **one symbol**, not the class. Questions
   about `risk`, `hotspots`, `reach`, `instability` and `gitlog` are still below the fold.
2. **The questions are targeted; the output is a ranking.** "Does `risk.py` import
   `hotspots`?" is a lookup, and a top-N cannot serve a lookup.
3. **Many are negative and exhaustive.** "Does *any* of graph/cycles/score/history/trend
   reach `layers`?" A digest can never answer a negative.
4. **The largest cluster is documentation content**: which line of README says what.
   `77 doc file(s)` is a count.

One blocker is self-inflicted and worth stating plainly: one of the 24 asks where test
helpers live and how they are named. Test modules are set aside by default, so the report
**structurally cannot answer it**. That default is right for a vendored legacy subtree
and wrong here, and at the time of the scoring `--include-tests` existed with nothing
pointing a reader at it. The report now prints `(--include-tests to census them)` beside
the excluded count, and truncated sections now name `--top`.

⚠️ **The 0 of 24 was measured before those two fixes and has not been re-scored.** So it
describes the build the readers saw, not this one, and nothing here claims the fixes move
it. The honest prior is that they do not move it much: blockers 2, 3 and 4 above are
untouched by a hint, and a re-score would be the way to find out rather than an argument
about it.

**So the next change to this command is not a fifth census.** It is queryability: a
`--module` filter, an exhaustive mode, or a lookup that answers "what consumes X" and
"does X reach Y" on demand. 🔴 **And that should not be added to this PR**: the held-out
set scores detection, so a retrieval feature would ship unmeasured, which is the failure
this file exists to prevent. It needs its own held-out measurement, against derivations
rather than repositories.

**Update: `--module` shipped in [#414](https://github.com/hslee16/archy/pull/414), and the
measurement above is still owed.** The paragraph's first instruction held (it was kept out
of #412 and landed in its own PR), the second did not: there is no held-out score for
retrievability, so nothing here says the lookup answers the derivations it was built for.
The numbers in this file score DETECTION and are unaffected by it, which is exactly why
they cannot be read as evidence for it. Tracked as
[#418](https://github.com/hslee16/archy/issues/418).

it. The honest prior is that they do not move it much: blockers 2, 3 and 4 above are
untouched by a hint, and a re-score would be the way to find out rather than an argument
about it.

`--module` filter, an exhaustive mode, or a lookup that answers "what consumes X" and

rather than repositories.

of #412 and landed in its own PR), the second did not: there is no held-out score for
retrievability, so nothing here says the lookup answers the derivations it was built for.

they cannot be read as evidence for it. Tracked as

1. **What it measures**
   - It tests agents on iterative, long-horizon coding. There are 36 problems with 196 checkpoints, and at each checkpoint the agent extends its own earlier code as the spec changes (https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.24755).

   - Correctness is scored only by tests, with no LLM judge or human rating. Tests run against the program through a subprocess or its API and come in four kinds: core, error, hidden functionality, and regression. The metrics are Strict (all tests pass), Iso (all tests except regression pass) and Core (https://arxiv.org/html/2603.24755).
   - Quality is two static metrics, both calculated separately from correctness:
     - **Erosion:** the share of total "complexity mass" that sits in functions with cyclomatic complexity above 10, where mass = CC × √SLOC (Radon's cutoff).
     - **Verbosity:** the share of lines flagged by AST-grep rules or detected as clones (same URL).
   - Headline result: the best agent strictly passes 14.8% of checkpoints, and no agent solves any problem from start to finish (https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.24755).

2. **Use case and access**
   - It targets coding agents running in their own harnesses (Claude Code, Codex, Cursor CLI and others), each run in a fresh Docker container per checkpoint with a 2-hour limit (https://arxiv.org/html/2603.24755, https://www.scbench.ai/leaderboard).
   - It comes from SprocketLab at UW-Madison, led by Gabriel Orlanski. The paper was submitted 25 Mar 2026 (v2 on 7 May 2026) under CC BY 4.0. The harness is MIT-licensed and runs locally with Python 3.12+, Docker and an API key (https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.24755, https://github.com/SprocketLab/slop-code-bench).
   - Problems live in a separate repo and are also published as a Harbor dataset (https://github.com/gabeorlanski/scb-problems). Snorkel hosts a mirror leaderboard (https://snorkel.ai/blog/slopcodebench-measuring-code-erosion-as-agents-iterate/).

3. **Structural measures**
   - Both quality metrics work at the function level only: complexity concentration and duplication. Nothing I found measures layer violations, import cycles, coupling, module dependencies or architecture erosion in that sense (https://arxiv.org/html/2603.24755). The absence is UNVERIFIED beyond the paper and README.
   - The paper argues it targets maintainability and design decisions, but measures them only through those two metrics (same URL).

4. **Python, and whether an import-graph tool could matter**
   - Yes, Python: "We evaluate only on Python due to cost," and agent code was compared with 473 Python repositories (https://arxiv.org/html/2603.24755).
   - Solutions are written from scratch and grow over 3 to 8 checkpoints, and file layout is left to the agent. They are not existing large repos. Whether solutions become multi-file enough for blast-radius analysis to matter is UNVERIFIED, since I found no statistics on files per solution.

5. **Cost**
   - Opus 4.6 in Claude Code: about $3.17 per checkpoint and $620.80 for the full suite.
   - Opus 4.5: about $2.53 per checkpoint, $492.40 for the suite.
   - Opus 4.7: about $2.17 per checkpoint, $425.34 for the suite.
   - Sonnet 4.6: about $1.96 per checkpoint, $383.83 for the suite.
   - Source: Table 1 (https://arxiv.org/html/2603.24755). The leaderboard's highest-ranked run, GPT 5.5 in Codex, costs $1.51 per checkpoint (https://www.scbench.ai/leaderboard).

6. **Do extra context tools change scores?**
   - The paper tests no MCP servers, repo maps or code graphs that I could find. The only interventions are two prompts, "anti-slop" and "plan-first." These lowered starting erosion and verbosity but did not stop the decline, and correctness held flat or dropped. For example, GPT 5.3 Codex with anti-slop: erosion fell from 0.64 to 0.42 while Iso fell from 26.0 to 23.5 (https://arxiv.org/html/2603.24755). That pattern matches the delivery-line nulls in archy's own WHAT_DIDNT_WORK.
   - The lead author says in an interview that he relies on skills and subagents rather than extra tooling (https://snorkel.ai/blog/slopcodebench-measuring-code-erosion-as-agents-iterate/).
   - Any published result on context tools: UNVERIFIED (none found).</result>

**Closed 2026-07-26: archy is no longer under active development.**

The research line this ticket belongs to reached its conclusion. Three pre-registered claims, three nulls:

| measurement | subject | rate |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 25 live agent runs, riskiest SWE-bench tasks (#356) | cycles or declared-layer violations | **0%** (95% upper bound 12%) |
| 1,072 human commits, 11 repos (Q1a) | cycles introduced | **0.5%** per commit |
| 151 commit pairs in declaring projects (#359) | contract violations | **0.66%** per commit |
| 107 samples of those projects over time (#364) | rules going stale, coverage eroding | **null on all four pre-registered signals** |

The problem is real and rare, for agents and humans alike. Nobody has measured the cost of one occurrence, so "rare but expensive" is a hypothesis rather than a defence. Alongside that: ADOPTERS.md is empty and not one of 96+ issues came from outside.

Write-up: `docs/WHAT_DIDNT_WORK.md`. The README now leads with the retraction.

Closed rather than left open so nobody, including a future me, restarts from a premise that has been measured and failed. Reopen only with a reason that is not "maybe a different corpus."

#403 and #480 are now closed. I rejected SlopCodeBench (#480) because there's no way to use it that both fits what archy does and is likely to show something new:

**1. It measures a different layer of structure than archy.** It scores two things on agent code as it grows:
- **Erosion:** how much of the code's complexity sits in functions with cyclomatic complexity over 10.
- **Verbosity:** clones and lines flagged by AST-grep rules.

Both are function-level. archy works at module level: imports, layers, cycles, coupling, blast radius. The overlap is small. archy already reports function complexity in `hotspots` and clones in `duplicates`, but it doesn't prevent either.

**2. Its tasks give archy almost nothing to do.** Each task is a small program the agent writes from scratch and then extends over 3 to 8 checkpoints. There are no declared layers, so `check` has nothing to enforce. The agent wrote every file in the same session, so blast radius and affected-tests analysis tell it little.

**3. Using it to validate archy would be a seventh delivery intervention.** That means running agents with and without archy's MCP server and comparing scores, at roughly $400 to $600 per arm per full suite. AGENTS.md says a seventh attempt at pushing a fact to the model needs a reason it differs from the first six. Nothing here differs. The paper's own interventions ("anti-slop" and "plan-first" prompts) lowered erosion at the start but didn't stop it rising, and correctness held flat or dropped. That's the same pattern archy saw six times.

**4. No usage signal and an anti-theater fail.** No user has asked for it, and "run archy on a new benchmark from a paper" is exactly the shape that test exists to catch.

**Where the rejection is weakest:** one angle costs nothing. If SlopCodeBench publishes the agents' solutions at each checkpoint, `archy cycles` could be run over them with no agent time. - **Prior results:** 0% cycles in 25 live agent runs (#356) and 0.5% per human commit, and these solutions are small, so the expected answer is "nothing happens".
- **The #361 reopen bar:** #361 was closed with "reopen only with a reason that is not 'maybe a different corpus'".

I didn't check whether those solutions are actually published. If you think the iterative setting is a different enough reason, that's the one experiment I'd run, and it's cheap.

- **#418:** left open, as you chose.

input.description: Read issue #387

content.content:
Filed from an external bug report: a production incident where `python -m commands.setup_user` crashed because that entrypoint never reached the SQLAlchemy model registry. The registry has to be imported before first mapper configuration, or string-based relationship resolution fails. 11 of 34 sibling command modules imported it; 23 did not. The fix works through `commands/__init__.py`, so the reaching import is transitive, never direct.

archy would not have *found* that bug (see "The honest limit"). The question this ticket answers is what archy is missing that would have caught the other 21 latent instances once someone knew to look, and what would have surfaced it cold.

## 1. Required-reach contracts (the piece that matters)

The inverse of a forbid rule. Today `archy.yaml` can only say "A must not reach B". There is no way to say "A must reach B".

```yaml
required:
  - source: commands.**
    must_reach: core.database.model_registry
    reason: standalone entrypoints need the full mapper registry
```

**It must be transitive reach, not direct import.** `commands.setup_user` reaches the registry via `commands/__init__.py`. A direct-import rule flags all 34 correctly-fixed command modules as violations, which is worse than no rule.

Cost note, and a correction to the report's estimate. The report assumes archy "already computes transitive reach for forbidden edges, so required-reach is the same query negated". Half true:

- `archy check` (`layers.py`) is **direct edges only** - that is the subject of #343.

content.content:
"""Reach queries over an import graph: propagation cost, and the implicit
package-`__init__` edges any transitive-reach question needs.

MacCormack propagation cost and per-module reverse-reach fractions.

For an internal subgraph with `N` modules, propagation cost is the fraction
of the system that, on average, can be affected by a change to a randomly
chosen module. Formally:

    propagation_cost = sum over internal nodes of `|reverse_closure(n)|` / N^2

where `reverse_closure(n)` is the set of internal modules that transitively
import `n` (so a change to `n` could ripple to them) together with `n`
itself. External nodes are excluded because they are not subject to edits
inside the project.

Per-module value `propagation_cost[n] = |reverse_closure(n)| / N` is the
fraction of the project that depends on `n`. This is the per-module
"blast radius" for editing `n`, useful as an agent-facing diagnostic. The
project-level value equals the mean of the per-module values.

Empirically the most-validated single architectural metric in the
defect-prediction literature: multiple Spearman-significant studies
linking low propagation cost to lower bug rate and lower maintenance
cost, starting with MacCormack-Rusnak-Baldwin (2006) and replicated in
the 2026 architectural-technical-debt literature.

See `docs/research/RESEARCH_METRICS.md` section 3 for the relationship to Lakos's
NCCD (same metric family, different normalization).

archy:owns        compute_propagation_cost, package_init_edges, with_package_init_edges
"""

from __future__ import annotations

import networkx as nx


def compute_propagation_cost(graph: nx.DiGraph) -> tuple[float, dict[str, float]]:
    """Return (project_propagation_cost, per_module_fractions).

    Operates on internal nodes only (`external=True` nodes are excluded).
    A graph with zero internal nodes returns `(0.0, {})`; single-node
    cases return `1.0` per the natural formula because the one node IS
    the whole project.
    """
    internal = {n for n, d in graph.nodes(data=True) if not d.get("external")}
    n = len(internal)
    if n == 0:
        return 0.0, {}

    per_module: dict[str, float] = {}

"""Reach queries over an import graph: propagation cost, and the implicit
package-`__init__` edges any transitive-reach question needs.

MacCormack propagation cost and per-module reverse-reach fractions.

For an internal subgraph with `N` modules, propagation cost is the fraction
of the system that, on average, can be affected by a change to a randomly
chosen module. Formally:

    propagation_cost = sum over internal nodes of `|reverse_closure(n)|` / N^2

where `reverse_closure(n)` is the set of internal modules that transitively
import `n` (so a change to `n` could ripple to them) together with `n`
itself. External nodes are excluded because they are not subject to edits
inside the project.

Per-module value `propagation_cost[n] = |reverse_closure(n)| / N` is the
fraction of the project that depends on `n`. This is the per-module
"blast radius" for editing `n`, useful as an agent-facing diagnostic. The
project-level value equals the mean of the per-module values.

Empirically the most-validated single architectural metric in the
defect-prediction literature: multiple Spearman-significant studies
linking low propagation cost to lower bug rate and lower maintenance
cost, starting with MacCormack-Rusnak-Baldwin (2006) and replicated in
the 2026 architectural-technical-debt literature.

See `docs/research/RESEARCH_METRICS.md` section 3 for the relationship to Lakos's
NCCD (same metric family, different normalization).

archy:owns        compute_propagation_cost, package_init_edges, with_package_init_edges
"""

from __future__ import annotations

import networkx as nx


def compute_propagation_cost(graph: nx.DiGraph) -> tuple[float, dict[str, float]]:
    """Return (project_propagation_cost, per_module_fractions).

    Operates on internal nodes only (`external=True` nodes are excluded).
    A graph with zero internal nodes returns `(0.0, {})`; single-node
    cases return `1.0` per the natural formula because the one node IS
    the whole project.
    """
    internal = {n for n, d in graph.nodes(data=True) if not d.get("external")}
    n = len(internal)
    if n == 0:
        return 0.0, {}

    per_module: dict[str, float] = {}
    total = 0
    for node in internal:
        ancestors = nx.ancestors(graph, node) & internal
        # Reverse closure includes the node itself, so an isolated module
        # contributes 1/N rather than 0 to propagation cost.
        reach = len(ancestors) + 1
        per_module[node] = reach / n
        total += reach

behaviorally coupled", so this script does NOT prove precision. It measures two
things that DO inform the defaults:

  count falls as `--min-support` and `--min-confidence` rise, so the default
  sits where coincidental low-support pairs have dropped but genuine coupling
  remains.
* **Source/test composition** - each surfaced pair is classified src<->src /
  src<->test / test<->test (reusing the #247 `duplicates.is_test_path`), to
  decide whether source<->test co-change (a test changing with the module it
  tests) is signal worth keeping or noise to scope out by default.

The accuracy half is a manual spot-check (top pairs on a diverse trio,
hand-classified genuine-vs-coincidental) recorded alongside in
`bench/coupling_results.md`.

    uv run --with pyyaml python bench/coupling_sweep.py --stdout

import datetime as dt

import sys

)


def _column(rows: list[dict], key: tuple[int, float], field: str) -> list[int]:
    """The per-project values of one composition field at one grid cell."""

    ta, tb = is_test_path(path_a), is_test_path(path_b)

content.content:
The gap is real and measured. Of six agent patches on tasks naming all three of
archy's surfaces, **exactly one touched `mcp.py`**; a separate count over 25
cells found **seven that modified `layers.py` and wired nothing at all**. Every
one was pytest-green, because nothing in the suite asserts the mirror. I have
now made the same mistake myself twice in one week, in #421 and again in #426.

So [#429](https://github.com/hslee16/archy/issues/429) proposed that `archy
check` say so unasked: for a symbol the diff changed, find its callers, group
them by module, and name the caller modules the diff did not touch. The mirror
relation derived from the graph rather than declared in config.

**Pre-registered before the harness existed** ([`research/MIRROR_SURFACE_PRECISION.md`](research/MIRROR_SURFACE_PRECISION.md),
committed in `a20d22f`): precision **>= 0.70** over at least 20 firings, an
underpowered pass explicitly not a pass, and a miss means it does not ship.

**Measured over all 287 non-merge commits of archy's own history: 42 firings, 1
true positive, precision 0.024.** The threshold was missed by a factor of
thirty.

It is not the oracle's fault, which is worth saying because the oracle was
designed to be the suspect. It scores a firing true only if a later commit went
back and touched the named module for that symbol, so an omission nobody ever
fixed reads as a false positive, biasing against the feature by construction.
But the false positives are not uncorrected bugs. They look like this:

```
load_config changed in layers.py; cli.py updated, contracts.py NOT updated
LayerConfig changed in layers.py; cli.py updated, diff.py NOT updated
compute_score changed in score.py; cli.py updated, diff.py NOT updated
```

`contracts.py` calls `load_config`. It does not mirror it. Nothing about
`load_config` changing obliges any of its callers to change, and that is true of
almost every caller of almost every symbol.

**The finding, in one line: "caller" is the wrong relation.** A mirror is a
narrow thing, a set of surfaces that must all be updated when a finding kind is
added. Callers are a much wider set, and they are dominated by ordinary
consumers. The proposal conflated the two, and the graph as archy builds it
cannot tell them apart, because it records that `contracts.py` calls
`layers.load_config`, not why.

Restricting to the `cli.py` / `mcp.py` pair, the two surfaces that really are
mirrors of each other, does not rescue it: **18 firings, 1 true positive,
precision 0.056.** That subgroup was computed after the fact and is reported
because the pre-registration asked for the false positives in full, not as a
result. It is not a rescued signal, it is the same null at higher resolution.

**What this does and does not settle.** It kills the derivation #429 proposed.
It does not touch the census that motivated it: the omissions are real, they are
frequent, and pytest is green through all of them. A narrower relation, say
"symbols reached by the same renderer family that `archy conventions` already
detects as a mirrored surface", is a **different hypothesis** and would need its
own pre-registration and its own pilot. Writing that sentence is not permission
to go and fit one to this data.

Two harness bugs were caught before the number existed, both by the smoke run
that AGENTS.md requires. The first version matched symbol names as substrings
and reported 42 firings at precision 0.038, every one vocabulary collision: the
CLI commands are called `check`, `diff` and `snapshot`, so any module containing
the word "check" scored as a caller of `cli.check`. The second returned module
names without their package prefix, so no import ever matched and the detector
fired zero times on every input, which is indistinguishable from a clean
history. `bench/mirror_precision.py --canary` now asserts the resolver still
sees two known cross-surface symbols, because both bugs produced a publishable
looking number.

[`bench/mirror_precision.py`]: ../bench/mirror_precision.py

## Study 8: pushing the fact at the model costs more, twice

# Mirror-surface detection: precision pre-registration (#429)

**Status: PRE-REGISTERED, NOT YET RUN.** Written before the harness exists and
before any number is known. Nothing in this file has been changed to fit a
result. If it is edited after the run, the edit is an amendment and says so.

## Why this file exists before the feature

[#429](https://github.com/hslee16/archy/issues/429) proposes that `archy check`
report, unasked, when a change updated a producer symbol and did not update the
surfaces that mirror it. Its own pre-registration clause says the precision
pilot runs **before any behaviour ships**, and this repository has a cautionary
case for doing it the other way round: [#369](https://github.com/hslee16/archy/issues/369)
fixed a win condition against a control rate inferred from a paper, and the
measured control rate made the win arithmetically unreachable before the run
started. Nobody noticed until afterwards.

So the order here is: thresholds, then reachability arithmetic, then harness,
then run, then decide. **A feature that misses the threshold does not ship**,
and the null goes in [`../WHAT_DIDNT_WORK.md`](../WHAT_DIDNT_WORK.md) with the
other four.

## What the detector will do

For a diff (a dirty tree, or `--since <ref>`):

1. Find the symbols the diff changed.
2. For each changed symbol, find its callers in the call graph archy already
   builds, and group them by the module they live in.
3. Report the caller modules the diff did **not** touch.

The mirror relation is **derived, never configured**. A config listing
`cli.py` and `mcp.py` as mirrors of each other would be a rule the maintainer
declared, which is the thing archy already does with `archy.yaml`; the claim
here is that the relation can be read off the graph.

## Definitions, fixed now

- **Producer symbol.** A top-level function or class defined in a module that
  the diff modified.
- **Caller module.** A module with a call or import edge into that symbol.
- **Candidate.** A `(commit, symbol)` pair where the symbol has caller modules
  in **two or more** distinct modules, at least one of which the commit touched.
  A symbol with one caller module has no mirror to be missing.
- **Firing.** A `(commit, symbol, module)` triple where `module` is a caller
  module the commit did not touch, and the commit touched at least one other
  caller module of that symbol. The asymmetry is the signal: updating one
  caller and not another is what "did not propagate" means.
- **Unit of analysis:** the firing. Precision is over firings, not commits,
  because one commit can fire on several symbols and a reader sees each line.

## The oracle, and its known bias

Labelling by hand would mean grading my own detector, so the label is
mechanical and comes from the repository's own future:

- **True positive:** within the next **5 commits** on the same branch lineage, a
  commit modifies the named module *and* its diff text mentions the symbol (or
  the symbol's name appears in the added/removed lines). The omission was real
  and somebody later had to go back and fix it.

# Mirror-surface detection: precision pre-registration (#429)

**Status: PRE-REGISTERED, NOT YET RUN.** Written before the harness exists and
before any number is known. Nothing in this file has been changed to fit a
result. If it is edited after the run, the edit is an amendment and says so.

## Why this file exists before the feature

[#429](https://github.com/hslee16/archy/issues/429) proposes that `archy check`
report, unasked, when a change updated a producer symbol and did not update the
surfaces that mirror it. Its own pre-registration clause says the precision
pilot runs **before any behaviour ships**, and this repository has a cautionary
case for doing it the other way round: [#369](https://github.com/hslee16/archy/issues/369)
fixed a win condition against a control rate inferred from a paper, and the
measured control rate made the win arithmetically unreachable before the run
started. Nobody noticed until afterwards.

So the order here is: thresholds, then reachability arithmetic, then harness,
then run, then decide. **A feature that misses the threshold does not ship**,
and the null goes in [`../WHAT_DIDNT_WORK.md`](../WHAT_DIDNT_WORK.md) with the
other four.

## What the detector will do

For a diff (a dirty tree, or `--since <ref>`):

1. Find the symbols the diff changed.
2. For each changed symbol, find its callers in the call graph archy already
   builds, and group them by the module they live in.
3. Report the caller modules the diff did **not** touch.

The mirror relation is **derived, never configured**. A config listing
`cli.py` and `mcp.py` as mirrors of each other would be a rule the maintainer
declared, which is the thing archy already does with `archy.yaml`; the claim
here is that the relation can be read off the graph.

## Definitions, fixed now

- **Producer symbol.** A top-level function or class defined in a module that
  the diff modified.
- **Caller module.** A module with a call or import edge into that symbol.
- **Candidate.** A `(commit, symbol)` pair where the symbol has caller modules
  in **two or more** distinct modules, at least one of which the commit touched.
  A symbol with one caller module has no mirror to be missing.
- **Firing.** A `(commit, symbol, module)` triple where `module` is a caller
  module the commit did not touch, and the commit touched at least one other
  caller module of that symbol. The asymmetry is the signal: updating one
  caller and not another is what "did not propagate" means.
- **Unit of analysis:** the firing. Precision is over firings, not commits,
  because one commit can fire on several symbols and a reader sees each line.

## The oracle, and its known bias

Labelling by hand would mean grading my own detector, so the label is
mechanical and comes from the repository's own future:

- **True positive:** within the next **5 commits** on the same branch lineage, a
  commit modifies the named module *and* its diff text mentions the symbol (or
  the symbol's name appears in the added/removed lines). The omission was real
  and somebody later had to go back and fix it.

"""Shared helpers for the bench sweep scripts.

Extracted so `hotspots_sweep.py` and `duplicates_sweep.py` (and any future
sweep) share one manifest loader and one clone/checkout routine instead of
copy-pasting them. Sweep scripts are run as `python bench/<name>.py`, so
`bench/` is on `sys.path[0]` and this module imports as `from _common import ...`.

archy:owns        clone_or_update, load_manifest
"""

from __future__ import annotations

import subprocess
from pathlib import Path

import yaml  # type: ignore[import-untyped]

REPO_ROOT = Path(__file__).resolve().parent.parent
MANIFEST = REPO_ROOT / "bench" / "projects.yaml"
WORKDIR = Path("/tmp/archy_bench")


def load_manifest() -> list[dict]:
    return yaml.safe_load(MANIFEST.read_text())["projects"]


def clone_or_update(proj: dict) -> Path | None:
    """Clone/checkout a project at its pinned SHA; never raises -- on any failure
    return None so the caller can skip the project and keep the sweep going. The
    archy self-entry uses REPO_ROOT directly (its pin may name a tag that does
    not exist yet during a release PR)."""
    name = proj["name"]
    sha = proj["sha"]
    if name == "archy":
        return REPO_ROOT
    target = WORKDIR / name
    if not target.exists():
        WORKDIR.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
        res = subprocess.run(
            ["git", "clone", "--quiet", f"https://github.com/{proj['repo']}.git", str(target)],
        )
        if res.returncode != 0:
            return None
    has_sha = subprocess.run(
        ["git", "-C", str(target), "cat-file", "-e", sha],
        capture_output=True,
    )
    if has_sha.returncode != 0:
        subprocess.run(["git", "-C", str(target), "fetch", "--quiet", "origin"], check=False)
    if (
        subprocess.run(
            ["git", "-C", str(target), "checkout", "--quiet", sha],
        ).returncode
        != 0
    ):
        return None
    subprocess.run(["git", "-C", str(target), "reset", "--hard", "--quiet", sha], check=False)
    subprocess.run(["git", "-C", str(target), "clean", "-fdx", "--quiet"], check=False)
    return target

# Reach-asymmetry sensing: precision pre-registration (#387, item 4)

**Status: PRE-REGISTERED, NOT YET RUN.** Written before the harness exists and
before any number is known. Nothing in this file is changed to fit a result. If
it is edited after the run, the edit is an amendment and says so.

## Why this file exists before the feature

[#387](https://github.com/hslee16/archy/issues/387) item 4 proposes a sensor:
for each package, for each target, flag a split where some sibling modules reach
the target and the rest do not. Its motivating incident is a package of 34
command modules where 13 reached the SQLAlchemy model registry and 21 did not;
the 21 crashed when run as entrypoints. The ticket says the sensor ships only if
a precision pilot clears a threshold written down first, and that the pilot must
run on transitive **reach** (with package-`__init__` edges), not on direct
imports. The reporter measured why: on the one real sample, direct-import
asymmetry flags 23 modules where 21 were broken, and reach flags exactly the 21.

The same discipline as [`MIRROR_SURFACE_PRECISION.md`](MIRROR_SURFACE_PRECISION.md)
applies: thresholds, then population arithmetic, then harness, then run, then
decide. **A sensor that misses the threshold does not ship**, and the null goes
in [`../WHAT_DIDNT_WORK.md`](../WHAT_DIDNT_WORK.md).

## What the sensor does

On one snapshot of a project, with the graph built by `build_graph` and widened
by `reach.with_package_init_edges`:

1. Find each package with enough sibling modules to have a convention.
2. For each internal target outside that sibling set, compute which siblings
   reach it transitively.
3. Report the splits that are neither near-universal nor near-absent, naming the
   siblings that do not reach the target.

It cannot know which side of a split is right. The claim under test is that a
reported split is an inconsistency that the project itself later resolves.

## Definitions, fixed now

- **Graph.** `with_package_init_edges(build_graph(src_dir, max_modules=0))`,
  internal nodes only. Test modules (`duplicates.is_test_path` on the module's
  path) are dropped everywhere: as packages, as siblings and as targets.
- **Package `P` and siblings `S`.** `S` is the set of internal non-test modules
  whose parent qualname is `P` (direct children; a subpackage counts as a
  child). `P` qualifies when `|S| >= 6`.
- **Target `T`.** Any internal non-test module that is not `P`, not an ancestor
  package of `P`, and not in `S`. Siblings are excluded as targets. Every
  sibling reaches `P` and its ancestors through the package-`__init__` edges, so
  those are uninformative by construction.
- **Reach set.** `R(T) = {s in S : T in descendants(s)}`; `k = |R|`, `n = |S|`.
- **Candidate split.** `0.2 <= k/n <= 0.8` and `min(k, n - k) >= 2`. The
  motivating incident (13 of 34, 0.38) is inside the band.
- **Firing (the unit of analysis).** Within one package, candidate targets with
  an identical reach set are one firing. Transitive chains otherwise turn a
  single convention into a dozen lines with the same modules on each side, and a
  reader sees one line, not twelve. A firing is `(P, R, targets)`; its
  **missing set** is `M = S \ R`.
- **Snapshots.** For each project in `bench/projects.yaml`, `T1` is the pinned
  SHA and `T0` is the last first-parent commit dated at least **365 days**
  before `T1`. The sensor runs at `T0`; the oracle reads `T1`. A project whose
  `src_dir` does not exist at `T0` is skipped and listed.

## The oracle, and its known biases

Labelling by hand would mean grading my own detector, so the label is
mechanical and comes from the project's own future, as in the mirror study.

For a firing at `T0`, let `M'` be the members of `M` that still exist at `T1`
under the same qualname, and `T*` the firing's targets that still exist at `T1`.

- **Unscorable** if `M'` or `T*` is empty. These are dropped and counted. Per
  AGENTS.md, an unmeasurable unit is never scored clean.
- **True positive (propagation)** if at least one module in `M'` reaches at least
  one target in `T*` at `T1`. The convention spread to a module that lacked it.
- **False positive** otherwise.

**Reported alongside, not gating: retraction.** The split also resolves if no
surviving member of `R` reaches any target in `T*` at `T1`. That is counted and
shown separately. It is not folded into the headline, because modules routinely
stop reaching things for reasons unrelated to any convention.

**Biases, stated in advance:**

1. **It undercounts real inconsistencies.** A gap nobody fixed within a year
   scores as a false positive. This biases against the sensor, which is the safe
   direction for a gate.
2. **It overcounts through ordinary growth.** Modules accumulate imports over a
   year, and "at least one of the missing modules gained reach" can happen by
   chance, especially for a widely used target. This biases toward the sensor,
   and the control below exists to measure it.
3. **One year is arbitrary.** It is fixed here and not tuned afterwards.

## The control

The same oracle is applied to **below-band** splits at `T0`: target classes
with `1 <= k` and `k/n < 0.2`, grouped by identical reach set in the same way.
Their propagation rate is the base rate at which a missing module gains reach to
something only a few siblings reach, which is the chance level that bias 2 adds
to the firings.

## Pre-registered thresholds

The sensor ships only if **all three** hold:

1. **Precision >= 0.40** over scorable firings (propagation only). The figure is
   a lower bound because of bias 1. It is set below the 0.70 used for the mirror
   sensor because this one would be an advisory list in a report a person asks
   for, not a line printed unasked on every `check`. It is set above what the
   duplicates sensor shipped at (~0.38 before its de-noiser) because that sensor
   had a semantic fix in prospect and this one does not.
2. **Lift >= 2.0**: firing precision is at least twice the control's propagation
   rate. Without this, a pass could be measuring that codebases grow.
3. **Power: >= 30 scorable firings from >= 5 projects.** Below that the run is
   underpowered and yields **no verdict**, which is not a pass. An underpowered
   pass does not ship.

**Reported alongside, not gates:** firings per project (a sensor that fires 300
times on one repository is noise even at good precision), the retraction count,
the unscorable count, the per-project precision, and at least ten false
positives in full so a reader can judge the oracle.

**Do not reinterpret these afterwards.** "Precision was 0.33 but the misses
were all test helpers" is a reinterpretation, not a result. A narrower sensor is
a different hypothesis and needs its own pre-registration.

## Harness canary

The harness must reproduce the incident before it is trusted. A synthetic
package of 34 modules, where 11 import a registry directly, 2 reach it through
an unrelated module and 21 do not, must produce exactly one firing for that
target. Its missing set must be the 21, and the 2 transitive reachers must sit
on the reaching side. A negative control removes one reaching edge and requires
the missing set to grow by one. If the canary fails, no number is reported.

## What a null means, and what it does not

A miss kills the sensor as specified. It does not touch items 1 and 2 of #387,
which shipped in v0.43.0 and are rules a maintainer writes, not inferences. It
also does not show that the incident was not real: the 21 modules crashed. A null
says only that "some siblings reach it and some do not" is too common a shape,
in ordinary codebases, to be worth printing.
